rows.stem: The specific sequence in which amino acids are arranged in a protein is called its
rows.solution:
The sequence of amino acids is the PRIMARY STRUCTURE of a protein.

The four levels are distinguished by what they describe and what holds them together. The PRIMARY structure is the order of the residues along the chain, fixed by peptide bonds — and it is the level that determines all the others, since the folding follows from the sequence.

The SECONDARY structure is how the chain arranges itself locally, as an \(\alpha\)-helix or a \(\beta\)-pleated sheet, held by hydrogen bonds between peptide linkages. The TERTIARY structure is the overall folding of the whole chain, and the QUATERNARY structure describes how several separate chains assemble, as the four subunits of haemoglobin do.

Denaturation destroys the secondary and tertiary structures while leaving the primary one intact — no peptide bond is broken.

rows.stem:
The correct name of the given reaction is
\(\mathrm{Ar-N_2^+\,X^-} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Cu\ CN/KCN}} \mathrm{Ar-CN + N_2}\)
rows.solution:
The reaction is SANDMEYER'S REACTION.

A diazonium salt is treated with a COPPER(I) SALT, and the diazonium group is replaced by whatever anion that salt brings — here cyanide, so the product is the nitrile and nitrogen escapes as a gas:
\(\mathrm{Ar{-}N_2^+X^-} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{CuCN}/\mathrm{KCN}} \mathrm{Ar{-}CN} + \mathrm{N_2}\)

Copper(I) chloride and bromide work the same way, giving the aryl chloride and bromide.

Of the others: Gabriel phthalimide synthesis makes primary ALIPHATIC amines from alkyl halides; the carbylamine reaction detects primary amines by the foul smell of the isocyanide; and Hofmann bromamide degradation converts an amide to an amine with one carbon fewer. None involves a diazonium salt.

rows.stem: Out of the following alkenes, the one which will produce tertiary butyl alcohol on acid catalysed hydration is
rows.solution:
The alkene is 2-METHYLPROPENE, \((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{C{=}CH_2}\).

Acid-catalysed hydration follows MARKOVNIKOV'S RULE: the proton adds to the doubly bonded carbon that already carries more hydrogens, so the hydroxyl goes to the OTHER one — the more substituted carbon.

Here the \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) end takes the proton and the hydroxyl goes to the carbon bearing the two methyl groups, which then carries three methyls and an \(-\mathrm{OH}\):
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{C{=}CH_2} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_2O}]{\mathrm{H^+}} (\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}OH}\)

That is tert-butyl alcohol, 2-methylpropan-2-ol. A TERTIARY alcohol requires the hydroxyl to land on a carbon already carrying three carbons, and only a branched alkene can supply one. The three straight-chain alkenes offered would give secondary alcohols.

rows.stem: Auto-oxidation of chloroform in air and light produces a poisonous gas known as
rows.solution:
The gas is PHOSGENE, \(\mathrm{COCl_2}\).

Chloroform is slowly oxidised by air in the presence of light:
\(2\mathrm{CHCl_3} + \mathrm{O_2} \xrightarrow{\text{light}} 2\mathrm{COCl_2} + 2\mathrm{HCl}\)

Phosgene, carbonyl chloride, is extremely poisonous — it was used as a war gas — which is why chloroform is stored in DARK bottles filled nearly to the top and closed tightly: the dark keeps the light out and the full bottle keeps the air out. About 1% ethanol is added as well, which destroys any phosgene formed by converting it to harmless diethyl carbonate.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Transition metals are known to make interstitial compounds. Formation of interstitial compounds makes the transition metal
rows.solution:
Forming interstitial compounds makes a transition metal MORE HARD.

An interstitial compound forms when small atoms — hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen or boron — occupy the INTERSTICES, the gaps between the metal atoms in the lattice. Being small, they fit without displacing anything.

Their presence makes it far harder for one layer of metal atoms to slide over another, and it is exactly that sliding which allows a metal to deform. Blocking it makes the metal harder and LESS ductile, and raises its melting point.

Steel is the everyday case: iron with a little carbon in its interstices is much harder than pure iron. The composition is usually non-stoichiometric, because the small atoms simply fill whatever gaps are available.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: Isotonic solutions have the same
rows.solution:
Isotonic solutions have the same OSMOTIC PRESSURE.

That is what the word means. Two solutions are isotonic when no net flow of solvent occurs between them across a semipermeable membrane — which happens precisely when their osmotic pressures are equal.

Since \(\Pi = iCRT\), two isotonic solutions at the same temperature also have the same concentration of PARTICLES, though not necessarily the same concentration of solute: a 0.9% sodium chloride solution is isotonic with blood, and so is a 5% glucose solution, because the salt supplies two particles per formula unit and the sugar one.

Density, refractive index and volume are all properties the two solutions may differ in freely.

rows.stem: Which of the following cell was used in Apollo space programme ?
rows.solution:
The APOLLO space programme used the \(\mathrm{H_2{-}O_2}\) FUEL CELL.

A fuel cell converts the energy of combustion of a fuel DIRECTLY into electrical energy, its reactants supplied continuously from outside rather than stored within, so it does not run down as long as it is fed.

Three things suited it to a spacecraft. Its efficiency is high, about 70%, because the energy does not pass through heat. It is pollution free, the only product being WATER — which on Apollo was drunk by the crew, so the by-product was itself a supply. And hydrogen and oxygen were already carried on board.

The other three are all storage cells with a fixed quantity of reactant sealed inside.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: The rate of a reaction increases sixteen times when the concentration of the reactant increases four times. The order of the reaction is
rows.solution:
The order is 2.0.

The rate responds to concentration as \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^n\), so multiplying the concentration by 4 multiplies the rate by \(4^n\):
\(16 = 4^{n}\)

and since \(16 = 4^2\), the order is 2.

Read the exponent off the numbers rather than guessing — the same method gives any order, whole or fractional. Note that the balanced equation could not have told us this; order is a property of the MECHANISM and has to be measured.

rows.stem: In which of the following molecules, C atom marked with asterisk is chiral ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the four candidate molecules (I), (II), (III), (IV) are printed as DRAWN wedge-and-dash 3-D structures around a starred carbon, and the four options are only lists of those Roman numerals, so the stem names nothing at all without them. The drawings are deliberately NOT described here: naming the four substituents on each starred carbon is exactly the discrimination the question tests, so a text rendering would state the answer. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
The chiral ones are I, II AND III.

A carbon is CHIRAL when it carries FOUR DIFFERENT groups — that is what makes the molecule non-superimposable on its mirror image. Check each starred carbon in turn.

I carries \(\mathrm{H}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3}\), \(\mathrm{Br}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl}\) — four different, so CHIRAL.
II carries \(\mathrm{D}\), \(\mathrm{I}\), \(\mathrm{Br}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl}\) — four different, so CHIRAL.
III carries \(\mathrm{D}\), \(\mathrm{OH}\), \(\mathrm{CH_2CH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_3}\) — four different, so CHIRAL.
IV carries \(\mathrm{H}\), \(\mathrm{D}\) and TWO \(\mathrm{CH_3}\) groups — the two methyls are IDENTICAL, so NOT chiral.

Structure II is worth pausing on: deuterium and hydrogen are different ISOTOPES of the same element, and that is enough to make them different groups. IV fails not on the isotopes but on the repeated methyl.

rows.stem: Which of the following species can act as the strongest base ?

options.label: D
options.text: The \(m\)-nitrophenoxide ion — a benzene ring bearing \(\mathrm{O^-}\), with \(\mathrm{O_2N}\) on the carbon META to it (drawn skeletal structure)

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — option (D) is a DRAWN benzene ring; options (A)-(C) are typeset formulas. Read at 3.5x: the ring carries \(\mathrm{O^-}\) at its right (mid-height) vertex and \(\mathrm{O_2N}\) at the bottom-left vertex, i.e. positions 1 and 3, so it is the m-nitrophenoxide ion. Naming it does NOT state the answer here (the question turns on comparing base strengths across all four species), so it is named in the option text as well; the crop should still be attached. Page idx 8.
rows.solution:
The strongest base is the ALKOXIDE ION, \(\mathrm{RO^-}\).

Base strength runs OPPOSITE to the acidity of the conjugate acid: the weaker the acid, the stronger the base it leaves behind. So rank the parent acids and reverse.

An ALCOHOL is the weakest acid of the set, \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) about 16, because its alkoxide has no way to spread the negative charge and the alkyl group pushes more density onto it. Water is next at 15.7. PHENOL is far stronger at about 10, its anion's charge being delocalised into the ring. And m-NITROPHENOL is stronger still at about 8.4, the nitro group withdrawing further.

Reversing that order puts the alkoxide first, then hydroxide, then phenoxide, with the nitrophenoxide the weakest base of the four.

rows.stem: Dilution affects both conductivity as well as molar conductivity. Effect of dilution on both is as follows :

options.label: C
options.text: conductivity increases whereas molar conductivity decreases on dilution.

options.label: D
options.text: conductivity decreases whereas molar conductivity increases on dilution.

rows.solution:
CONDUCTIVITY DECREASES whereas MOLAR CONDUCTIVITY INCREASES on dilution.

The two behave oppositely because they are referred to different things.

CONDUCTIVITY is the conductance of a fixed VOLUME — the solution held between electrodes one centimetre apart with an area of one square centimetre. Diluting puts fewer ions in that volume, so fewer charge carriers sit between the electrodes and the conductivity falls.

MOLAR CONDUCTIVITY refers the conductance to a fixed AMOUNT of electrolyte, one mole, however much solvent that mole is spread through:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{C}\)
Dilution lets the ions move apart, so they drag on one another less and — for a weak electrolyte — dissociate further. Both effects raise the value, and it climbs towards the limiting \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\).

rows.stem: Van’t Hoff factor for \(\mathrm{Na_2SO_4 \cdot 10H_2O}\) solution, assuming complete ionization is
rows.solution:
The van't Hoff factor is 3.

Sodium sulphate decahydrate dissolves and ionises as
\(\mathrm{Na_2SO_4} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Na^+} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\)
giving THREE particles from each formula unit.

The ten water molecules are WATER OF CRYSTALLISATION. On dissolving they simply join the bulk solvent — they do not become solute particles, and a colligative property counts only solute particles.

The distractor 13 is built by counting them, adding the ten waters to the three ions. That is the whole point of writing the formula as a hydrate.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Zr and Hf are of almost similar atomic radii.
Reason (R) : This is due to Lanthanoid contraction.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Zirconium and hafnium have almost identical atomic radii — about 160 pm each — although hafnium lies a whole period below zirconium and should therefore be considerably larger.

LANTHANOID CONTRACTION is exactly why. The fourteen lanthanoids come between them in the periodic table, and across that series the \(4f\) electrons shield the growing nuclear charge very poorly, so the radius shrinks steadily. That shrinkage very nearly cancels the increase the extra period would otherwise bring.

The practical consequence is that the two elements behave almost identically and are notoriously difficult to separate — chemical separation depends on differences in size and the properties that follow from it.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The units of rate constant of a zero order reaction and rate of reaction are the same.
Reason (R) : In zero order reaction, the rate of reaction is independent of the concentration of reactants.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

For a zero order reaction \(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^0 = k\). With the concentration term gone, the constant IS the rate, so the two necessarily carry the same units, \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\).

The Reason states precisely the condition that produces that identity: the rate being independent of concentration is what leaves \(k\) standing alone on the right-hand side.

Note that the marking scheme accepts BOTH "correct explanation" and "not the correct explanation" for this question — the two statements are close enough to being restatements of each other that CBSE allowed either reading. The bank's stored key is the former.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Inversion of configuration is observed in \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) reaction.
Reason (R) : The reaction proceeds with the formation of carbocation.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

Inversion of configuration IS observed in an \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction — the Walden inversion. The nucleophile attacks from the side directly OPPOSITE the leaving group, and the other three bonds are pushed through to the far side like an umbrella turning inside out, all in one step.

The Reason describes the OTHER mechanism. It is \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) that proceeds through a CARBOCATION, and that intermediate is exactly why \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) does NOT give inversion: the cation is planar, so the nucleophile attacks either face with equal ease and the product is racemic.

So the Reason, if it were true of this mechanism, would predict the opposite of the Assertion. An \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction has no intermediate at all — only a transition state in which the bond to the nucleophile is forming as the bond to the leaving group breaks.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : p-methoxyphenol is a stronger acid than p-nitrophenol.
Reason (R) : Methoxy group shows \(+\mathrm{I}\) effect whereas nitro group shows \(-\mathrm{I}\) effect.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is FALSE while the Reason is TRUE.

p-Methoxyphenol is a WEAKER acid than p-nitrophenol, not a stronger one — \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) about 10.2 against 7.1.

The Reason is correct in the sense the paper intends: the nitro group WITHDRAWS electron density while the methoxy group RELEASES it. And that is exactly why the Assertion fails. Acidity here depends on the stability of the PHENOXIDE ion: a withdrawing group disperses its negative charge and stabilises it, making the acid stronger, while a releasing group concentrates the charge and weakens the acid.

The methoxy group's dominant effect at the PARA position is donation by resonance, its lone pair feeding into the ring; its inductive pull runs the other way but is outweighed there.

So p-methoxyphenol is weaker even than phenol itself, while p-nitrophenol is nearly a thousandfold stronger.

rows.stem:
State :
(a) Kohlrausch law of independent migration of ions.
(b) Faraday’s first law of electrolysis.
rows.solution:
(a) KOHLRAUSCH'S LAW OF INDEPENDENT MIGRATION OF IONS states that the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the SUM of the individual contributions of its cation and anion:
\(\Lambda_m^{\circ} = \nu_+\lambda_+^{\circ} + \nu_-\lambda_-^{\circ}\)
where \(\lambda_+^{\circ}\) and \(\lambda_-^{\circ}\) are the limiting molar conductivities of the cation and anion, and \(\nu_+\) and \(\nu_-\) are how many of each the formula unit gives.

At infinite dilution the ions are so far apart that each moves entirely INDEPENDENTLY of the other, which is what makes the simple sum valid. Its great use is finding \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) for a WEAK electrolyte, which cannot be got by extrapolation.

(b) FARADAY'S FIRST LAW OF ELECTROLYSIS states that the amount of chemical reaction occurring at an electrode during electrolysis is DIRECTLY PROPORTIONAL to the quantity of electricity passed through the electrolyte.

In symbols \(m = ZIt\), where \(m\) is the mass deposited or liberated, \(Z\) the electrochemical equivalent of the substance, \(I\) the current and \(t\) the time.

rows.stem:
Classify the following sugars into monosaccharides and disaccharides :
Galactose, Glucose, Lactose and Maltose
rows.solution:
MONOSACCHARIDES: GALACTOSE and GLUCOSE.
DISACCHARIDES: LACTOSE and MALTOSE.

A monosaccharide is a single sugar unit and cannot be hydrolysed to anything simpler; a disaccharide is two such units joined by a glycosidic linkage, and hydrolysis splits it into two.

Note how the list is constructed: lactose hydrolyses to GLUCOSE and GALACTOSE, and maltose to two molecules of GLUCOSE — so both monosaccharides in the list are the building blocks of the disaccharides beside them.

All four are REDUCING sugars, each having an anomeric carbon free. Sucrose, which is not listed, is the one common disaccharide that is not.

rows.stem:
Carry out the following conversions :
(i) Nitrobenzene to Aniline
(ii) Aniline to Phenol
rows.solution:
(i) NITROBENZENE TO ANILINE, by reduction of the nitro group. Tin with hydrochloric acid is the standard laboratory method; iron with hydrochloric acid is preferred industrially, since the iron is regenerated by the acid and less of it is needed:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NO_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Sn}/\mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\)

Catalytic hydrogenation over palladium serves equally well when no other reducible group is present.

(ii) ANILINE TO PHENOL, in two steps by way of the diazonium salt. Nitrous acid generated in situ at 273-278 K diazotises the amine, and WARMING the salt with water replaces the diazonium group by a hydroxyl:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} \xrightarrow[273\text{-}278\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{NaNO_2}/\mathrm{HCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} \xrightarrow[\text{warm}]{\mathrm{H_2O}} \mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + \mathrm{N_2} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

The low temperature of the first step and the warming of the second are both essential — the salt decomposes above about 278 K, which is precisely what the second step exploits.

rows.stem:
(i) Write a chemical test to distinguish between Dimethyl amine and Ethanamine.
(ii) Write the product formed when benzene diazonium chloride is treated with KI.
rows.solution:
(i) Use the CARBYLAMINE TEST. Warm each with chloroform and alcoholic potassium hydroxide.

ETHANAMINE is a PRIMARY amine, with TWO hydrogens on its nitrogen, so it forms an isocyanide — detected at once by its exceptionally foul smell:
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{C_2H_5NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)

DIMETHYLAMINE is SECONDARY, with only ONE hydrogen on nitrogen where two are needed, so it gives no isocyanide and no smell.

Hinsberg's test distinguishes them too: the primary amine gives an alkali-soluble sulphonamide, the secondary one an insoluble one.

(ii) The product is IODOBENZENE.

Iodide is the one halide that needs no copper catalyst — simply warming the diazonium salt with potassium iodide suffices:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} + \mathrm{KI} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5I} + \mathrm{N_2} + \mathrm{KCl}\)

The chloride and bromide both require a copper(I) salt, the Sandmeyer reaction, and fluoride requires the quite different Balz-Schiemann route through the diazonium fluoroborate. Iodobenzene is thus the easiest aryl halide to make this way, and the route is the standard one since direct iodination of benzene is reversible and unsatisfactory.

rows.stem: Show that in case of a first order reaction, the time taken for completion of 99% reaction is twice the time required for 90% completion of the reaction. (log 10 = 1)
rows.solution:
Take the first order integrated rate equation and apply it twice.

FOR 99% COMPLETION. Let \([\mathrm{A}]_0 = 100\); then 99 has reacted and \([\mathrm{A}] = 1\):
\(t_{99\%} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k}\log\dfrac{100}{1} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k}\log 100 = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k} \times 2\)

FOR 90% COMPLETION. Let \([\mathrm{A}]_0 = 100\); then \([\mathrm{A}] = 10\):
\(t_{90\%} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k}\log\dfrac{100}{10} = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k}\log 10 = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{k} \times 1\)

DIVIDE the first by the second. Everything but the logarithms cancels — the rate constant along with the rest:
\(\dfrac{t_{99\%}}{t_{90\%}} = \dfrac{2}{1} = 2\)

so \(t_{99\%} = 2 \times t_{90\%}\), as required.

The cancellation of \(k\) is what makes the result general: it holds for EVERY first order reaction, fast or slow. The underlying reason is that going from 90% to 99% complete means the remaining tenth falls by a further factor of ten — one more decade, taking exactly as long as the first.

rows.stem: Resistance of a conductivity cell filled with \(0.2\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\) \(\mathrm{KCl}\) solution is \(200\ \Omega\). If the resistance of the same cell when filled with \(0.05\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\) \(\mathrm{KCl}\) solution is \(620\ \Omega\), calculate the conductivity and molar conductivity of \(0.05\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\) \(\mathrm{KCl}\) solution. The conductivity of \(0.2\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\) \(\mathrm{KCl}\) solution is \(0.0248\ \mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}\).
rows.solution:
The two measurements share one cell, so the potassium chloride solution of KNOWN conductivity is used to CALIBRATE it, and the dilute solution is then measured with the constant so obtained.

Step 1 — cell constant:
\(G^{*} = \kappa \times R = 0{\cdot}0248\ \mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}} \times 200\ \Omega\)
\(G^{*} = 4{\cdot}96\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}\)

The units confirm the step: siemens cancels ohm, leaving reciprocal centimetres, which is what a cell constant must be.

Step 2 — conductivity of the dilute solution, using the same constant with its own resistance:
\(\kappa = \dfrac{G^{*}}{R} = \dfrac{4{\cdot}96}{620}\)
\(\kappa = 0{\cdot}008\ \mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}\)

Step 3 — molar conductivity. Divide out the concentration to refer the conductivity to one mole of electrolyte:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{C} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}008 \times 1000}{0{\cdot}05}\)

\(\Lambda_m = 160\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

The result illustrates the previous question's point: the dilute solution has the SMALLER conductivity but the LARGER molar conductivity.

rows.stem:
Write the IUPAC names of the following coordination compounds (any three) :
(a) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl(NO_2)]Cl}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{[Ni(NH_3)_6]Cl_2}\)
(c) \(\mathrm{K_3[Cr(C_2O_4)_3]}\)
(d) \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_2Br_2]^+}\)
rows.solution:
(a) The chloride outside gives \(-1\), and inside the sphere four ammines are neutral while chlorido and nitro each give \(-1\), so cobalt is \(+3\). Ligands are named alphabetically — ammine, chlorido, nitro — and the nitrite bound through NITROGEN is named nitro-N:
TETRAAMMINECHLORIDONITRITO-N-COBALT(III) CHLORIDE

(b) Two chlorides outside give \(-2\) and six ammines are neutral, so nickel is \(+2\):
HEXAAMMINENICKEL(II) CHLORIDE

(c) Three potassiums give \(+3\) and three oxalato ligands \(-6\), so chromium is \(+3\) and the complex is the ANION — which takes the -ate ending:
POTASSIUM TRIOXALATOCHROMATE(III)

(d) Two bromido ligands give \(-2\) against an overall \(+1\), and the two diamines are neutral, so cobalt is \(+3\). The bracketed ligand takes bis- because its own name already contains a numerical prefix:
DIBROMIDOBIS(ETHANE-1,2-DIAMINE)COBALT(III) ION

rows.stem:
Give the structure of the major product expected from the following reactions :
(a) Reaction of Ethanal with methyl-magnesium bromide followed by hydrolysis.
(b) Hydration of But-1-ene in the presence of dilute sulphuric acid.
(c) Reaction of phenol with bromine water.
rows.solution:
(a) A Grignard reagent adds to the carbonyl carbon, and with an ALDEHYDE other than methanal the product after hydrolysis is a SECONDARY alcohol:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} \xrightarrow[2.\ \mathrm{H_3O^+}]{1.\ \mathrm{CH_3MgBr}} \mathrm{CH_3CH(OH)CH_3}\)
The product is PROPAN-2-OL. Counting carbons: two in the aldehyde plus one from the reagent gives three.

(b) Acid-catalysed hydration follows MARKOVNIKOV'S RULE — the proton adds to the carbon carrying more hydrogens, so the hydroxyl goes to the OTHER one:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH{=}CH_2} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_2O}]{\text{dil. }\mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH(OH)CH_3}\)
The product is BUTAN-2-OL, not butan-1-ol. Hydroboration-oxidation would give the primary alcohol instead.

(c) Bromine water substitutes at ALL THREE activated positions at once, giving a white precipitate:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + 3\mathrm{Br_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_2Br_3OH} + 3\mathrm{HBr}\)
The product is 2,4,6-TRIBROMOPHENOL — a benzene ring carrying \(-\mathrm{OH}\) with bromines at both ortho positions and the para position.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
Draw the structures of major product(s) in each of the following reactions :
(a) A cyclohexanone ring carrying a \(\mathrm{-CHO}\) group on the carbon para to the \(\mathrm{C=O}\) (4-oxocyclohexane-1-carbaldehyde) \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+\ OH^-}}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{(CH_3)(H)C=C(CH_3)-CO-CH_3}\) \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaOI}}\)
(c) A benzene ring carrying \(\mathrm{-CHO}\) and \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) on adjacent carbons (2-formylbenzoic acid) \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaCN/HCl}}\)
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — all three substrates are printed as DRAWN skeletal structures rather than named; only the reagent above each arrow is typeset. Read at 2.6x and named losslessly in the stem above, which is safe here because the question asks for the PRODUCTS, so naming the substrates leaks nothing. Marked REQUIRED rather than ILLUSTRATIVE because the drawings are the whole of what the stem supplies and the crops should certainly be attached. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
(a) Tollens' reagent is a MILD oxidising agent, and it is SELECTIVE: it oxidises an ALDEHYDE and leaves a KETONE alone.

The substrate carries both, so only the aldehyde is attacked — and since the reagent is alkaline the product is the CARBOXYLATE ion rather than the free acid.

Product: the cyclohexanone ring still carrying its \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\), with the \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) now a \(-\mathrm{COO^-}\) on the carbon para to it.

(b) Sodium hypoiodite is the IODOFORM reagent, and the substrate has the \(\mathrm{CH_3CO}-\) group it requires. The methyl carbon leaves as iodoform and the rest becomes the salt of the acid; the carbon-carbon double bond is untouched.

Products: \((\mathrm{CH_3})(\mathrm{H})\mathrm{C{=}C}(\mathrm{CH_3}){-}\mathrm{COONa}\), the sodium salt of 2-methylbut-2-enoic acid, together with \(\mathrm{CHI_3}\), the yellow precipitate of iodoform.

(c) Cyanide adds to the ALDEHYDE group to form a CYANOHYDRIN; the carboxyl group is not attacked, its carbon being far less electrophilic.

Product: the benzene ring keeping its \(-\mathrm{COOH}\), with the \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) on the adjacent carbon now \(-\mathrm{CH(OH)CN}\).

rows.stem:
Calculate the emf of the following cell :
\(\mathrm{Ni(s) + 2Ag^+(0.01\ M) \longrightarrow Ni^{2+}(0.1\ M) + 2Ag(s)}\)
Given that \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}_{cell}} = 1.05\) V, log 10 = 1
rows.solution:
The standard potential is given, so only the Nernst correction remains.

The reaction as written has nickel oxidised and silver deposited, and TWO electrons are transferred — one nickel giving up two, two silver ions taking one each — so \(n = 2\). Solids do not enter the quotient:
\(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{Ag^+}]^2}\)
\(= 1{\cdot}05 - \dfrac{0{\cdot}059}{2}\log\dfrac{0{\cdot}1}{(0{\cdot}01)^2}\)
\(= 1{\cdot}05 - 0{\cdot}0295 \times \log 10^{3}\)
\(= 1{\cdot}05 - 0{\cdot}0295 \times 3 = 1{\cdot}05 - 0{\cdot}0885\)

\(E_{\text{cell}} = 0{\cdot}9615\ \mathrm{V}\)

The SQUARED term is where this question can go wrong. \((0{\cdot}01)^2\) is \(10^{-4}\), so the quotient is \(10^{-1}/10^{-4} = 10^{3}\), not \(10\) — the silver ion's coefficient of 2 in the balanced equation carries through as an exponent in the Nernst quotient.

rows.stem:
Account for the following :
(a) Haloalkanes react with AgCN to form isocyanide as main product.
(b) Allyl chloride shows high reactivity towards \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction.
(c) Haloarenes are extremely less reactive towards nucleophilic substitution reactions.
rows.solution:
(a) Because SILVER CYANIDE IS MAINLY COVALENT, so the cyanide is not free to attack through its preferred atom.

In an ionic cyanide such as potassium cyanide the free \(\mathrm{CN^-}\) ion attacks through its CARBON, the better nucleophilic site, and the product is the NITRILE.

In silver cyanide the bond to the metal is largely covalent, and that ties up the carbon's lone pair. Only the NITROGEN is left free to donate, so attack occurs through nitrogen and the product is the ISOCYANIDE, \(\mathrm{R{-}NC}\).

One reagent gives the cyanide, the other the isocyanide, from the same halide — the difference lying entirely in how ionic the metal cyanide is.

(b) Because the ALLYL CARBOCATION is stabilised by RESONANCE.

The rate of an \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction is set by how easily the carbocation forms, since that is the slow step. Allyl chloride's chlorine sits on the carbon NEXT TO the double bond, so when the chloride leaves the positive charge is shared over TWO carbons by two equivalent resonance structures:
\(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CH{-}\overset{+}{C}H_2} \longleftrightarrow \mathrm{\overset{+}{C}H_2{-}CH{=}CH_2}\)

An ordinary primary halide gives a plain primary cation with no such help, so it reacts by this route far more slowly.

(c) Because the carbon-halogen bond in a haloarene is much harder to break.

The halogen's lone pair is delocalised INTO THE RING by resonance, so the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond acquires partial DOUBLE BOND character: it is shorter and stronger, and a bond with double bond character does not break to let a nucleophile substitute. The carbon carrying it is also \(sp^2\) rather than \(sp^3\), and an \(sp^2\) carbon holds the shared pair more tightly.

Two further factors point the same way: the ring's electron-rich \(\pi\) cloud REPELS an approaching nucleophile, and the PHENYL CATION that a unimolecular route would require is extremely unstable.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
The rate constant of a reaction quadruples when the temperature changes from 300 K to 320 K. Calculate the activation energy for this reaction.
[log 2 = 0.30, log 4 = 0.60, 2.303 R = 19.15 J \(\mathrm{K^{-1}mol^{-1}}\)]
rows.solution:
Two rate constants at two temperatures are related by the Arrhenius equation in its two-point form:
\(\log\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{2{\cdot}303\,R}\left[\dfrac{T_2 - T_1}{T_1 T_2}\right]\)

The constant QUADRUPLES, so \(k_2/k_1 = 4\) and \(\log 4 = 0{\cdot}60\), with \(T_1 = 300\) K and \(T_2 = 320\) K:
\(0{\cdot}60 = \dfrac{E_a}{19{\cdot}15}\left[\dfrac{320 - 300}{320 \times 300}\right] = \dfrac{E_a}{19{\cdot}15} \times \dfrac{20}{96000}\)

\(E_a = \dfrac{0{\cdot}60 \times 19{\cdot}15 \times 320 \times 300}{20}\)

\(E_a = 55152\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\), that is \(55{\cdot}152\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

Note that \(2{\cdot}303R\) is supplied as a single quantity, so it goes straight into the denominator without being split — and the temperatures must be in KELVIN, since their product appears in the bracket.

rows.stem: A compound ‘X’ with molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_3H_9N}\) reacts with \(\mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2Cl}\) to give a solid, insoluble in alkali. Identify ‘X’ and give the IUPAC name of the product. Write the reaction involved.
rows.solution:
The clue is the ALKALI-INSOLUBLE solid, which identifies the CLASS of amine at once.

Benzenesulphonyl chloride is Hinsberg's reagent. A SECONDARY amine gives a sulphonamide with NO hydrogen left on its nitrogen — both positions are taken by carbon groups and the third by the sulphonyl group — so there is nothing acidic for alkali to remove and the product is INSOLUBLE in alkali. A primary amine's product would dissolve; a tertiary amine would not react at all.

So \(\mathrm{X}\) is a SECONDARY amine of formula \(\mathrm{C_3H_9N}\). With three carbons distributed over two groups on the nitrogen, the only possibility is a methyl and an ethyl:
\(\mathrm{X} = \mathrm{CH_3{-}NH{-}C_2H_5}\), N-methylethanamine

The reaction:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2Cl} + \mathrm{CH_3{-}NH{-}C_2H_5} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2{-}N(CH_3)(C_2H_5)} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

IUPAC name of the product: N-ETHYL-N-METHYLBENZENESULPHONAMIDE

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: Define ambidentate ligand with an example.
rows.context: The oxidation number of the central atom in a complex is defined as the charge it would carry if all the ligands are removed along with the electron pairs that are shared with the central atom. Similarly the charge on the complex is the sum of the charges of the constituent parts i.e. the sum of the charges on the central metal ion and its surrounding ligands. Based on this, the complex is called neutral if the sum of the charges of the constituents is equal to zero. However, for an anion or cationic complex, the sum of the charges of the constituents is equal to the charge on the coordination sphere.
rows.solution:
An AMBIDENTATE LIGAND is one with TWO DIFFERENT DONOR ATOMS, of which it binds the metal through only ONE AT A TIME.

Example: the NITRITE ion, \(\mathrm{NO_2^-}\). It may attach through its NITROGEN, giving the nitro form, or through an OXYGEN, giving the nitrito form — and the two are genuinely different compounds with different colours. The thiocyanate ion, \(\mathrm{SCN^-}\), behaves the same way, binding through sulphur or through nitrogen.

The choice gives rise to LINKAGE ISOMERISM. Note that ambidentate is not the same as BIDENTATE: a bidentate ligand uses two donor atoms AT ONCE, closing a chelate ring, whereas an ambidentate one merely has a choice between two.

rows.stem: What type of isomerism is shown by \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Cl]SO_4}\) and \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]Cl}\) ?
rows.context: The oxidation number of the central atom in a complex is defined as the charge it would carry if all the ligands are removed along with the electron pairs that are shared with the central atom. Similarly the charge on the complex is the sum of the charges of the constituent parts i.e. the sum of the charges on the central metal ion and its surrounding ligands. Based on this, the complex is called neutral if the sum of the charges of the constituents is equal to zero. However, for an anion or cationic complex, the sum of the charges of the constituents is equal to the charge on the coordination sphere.
rows.solution:
The pair shows IONISATION ISOMERISM.

Ionisation isomers contain the same atoms but exchange a LIGAND inside the coordination sphere for a COUNTER ION outside it. Here the chloride and the sulphate swap places: in one compound the chloride is the ligand and the sulphate the counter ion, in the other the reverse.

Because the two give DIFFERENT IONS in solution, they are easily told apart by simple tests. \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Cl]SO_4}\) releases the sulphate ion, so it gives a white precipitate with barium chloride; \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]Cl}\) releases the chloride ion, so it gives a white precipitate with silver nitrate. Each fails the other's test.

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: Define Chelate effect. How it affects the stability of complex ?
rows.context: The oxidation number of the central atom in a complex is defined as the charge it would carry if all the ligands are removed along with the electron pairs that are shared with the central atom. Similarly the charge on the complex is the sum of the charges of the constituent parts i.e. the sum of the charges on the central metal ion and its surrounding ligands. Based on this, the complex is called neutral if the sum of the charges of the constituents is equal to zero. However, for an anion or cationic complex, the sum of the charges of the constituents is equal to the charge on the coordination sphere.
rows.solution:
The CHELATE EFFECT is the extra stability a complex gains when a BIDENTATE OR POLYDENTATE ligand binds the metal through two or more donor atoms at once, closing a RING that includes the metal atom.

HOW IT AFFECTS STABILITY: it INCREASES it, and substantially. A chelated complex is far more stable than one formed by the same number of separate monodentate donors — \(\mathrm{[Ni(en)_3]^{2+}}\) is much more stable than \(\mathrm{[Ni(NH_3)_6]^{2+}}\), though both bind nickel through six nitrogens.

Two reasons. Once one donor atom of a chelating ligand has attached, the second is held close to the metal and binds readily, whereas a second separate ligand would have to arrive from the solution. And releasing a chelating ligand requires TWO bonds to break at once rather than one.

The more chelate rings, the greater the stability — which is why \(\mathrm{EDTA^{4-}}\), closing five of them, forms such exceptionally stable complexes.

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: Find the coordination number and oxidation state of chromium in \(\mathrm{Na_3[Cr(C_2O_4)_3]}\).
rows.context: The oxidation number of the central atom in a complex is defined as the charge it would carry if all the ligands are removed along with the electron pairs that are shared with the central atom. Similarly the charge on the complex is the sum of the charges of the constituent parts i.e. the sum of the charges on the central metal ion and its surrounding ligands. Based on this, the complex is called neutral if the sum of the charges of the constituents is equal to zero. However, for an anion or cationic complex, the sum of the charges of the constituents is equal to the charge on the coordination sphere.
rows.solution:
Work from the outside in. Three sodium ions give \(+3\), so the complex ion carries \(-3\).

OXIDATION STATE. Each oxalate ion is \(\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}}\), so three of them give \(-6\):
\(x + (-6) = -3\), giving \(x = +3\)
Chromium is in the \(+3\) oxidation state.

COORDINATION NUMBER. The oxalate ion is BIDENTATE — it binds through TWO of its oxygen atoms at once, closing a five-membered chelate ring. Three such ligands therefore supply
\(3 \times 2 = 6\) donor atoms

The coordination number is 6, and the complex is octahedral.

Counting the three LIGANDS instead of the six donor atoms gives 3, which is the commonest error here.

rows.stem: What is the other name of vitamin \(\mathrm{B_6}\) ?
rows.context: Certain organic compounds are required in small amounts in our diet but their deficiency causes specific disease. These compounds are called vitamins. Most of the vitamins cannot be synthesized in our body but plants can synthesize almost all of them. So they are considered as essential food factors. However, the bacteria of the gut can produce some of the vitamins required by us. All the vitamins are generally available in our diet. The term ‘vitamin’ was coined from the words vital + amine, since the earlier identified compounds had amino group. Vitamins are classified into two groups depending upon their solubility in water or fat namely-fat soluble vitamins and water soluble vitamins.
rows.solution:
The other name of vitamin \(\mathrm{B_6}\) is PYRIDOXINE.

It is WATER SOLUBLE, like the rest of the B group, so the body cannot store a reserve of it and a regular dietary supply is needed. A deficiency causes convulsions.

rows.stem: Name the vitamin whose deficiency causes increased blood clotting time.
rows.context: Certain organic compounds are required in small amounts in our diet but their deficiency causes specific disease. These compounds are called vitamins. Most of the vitamins cannot be synthesized in our body but plants can synthesize almost all of them. So they are considered as essential food factors. However, the bacteria of the gut can produce some of the vitamins required by us. All the vitamins are generally available in our diet. The term ‘vitamin’ was coined from the words vital + amine, since the earlier identified compounds had amino group. Vitamins are classified into two groups depending upon their solubility in water or fat namely-fat soluble vitamins and water soluble vitamins.
rows.solution:
The vitamin is VITAMIN K.

It is needed to make several of the clotting factors, so a deficiency shows as an INCREASED CLOTTING TIME — cuts bleed for longer and bruising is easy.

Vitamin K is FAT SOLUBLE, so the body can store a reserve in the liver, which is why the deficiency develops slowly. Newborns, who have little, are routinely given a dose.

rows.stem: Xerophthalmia is caused by the deficiency of which vitamin ? Give two sources of this vitamin.
rows.context: Certain organic compounds are required in small amounts in our diet but their deficiency causes specific disease. These compounds are called vitamins. Most of the vitamins cannot be synthesized in our body but plants can synthesize almost all of them. So they are considered as essential food factors. However, the bacteria of the gut can produce some of the vitamins required by us. All the vitamins are generally available in our diet. The term ‘vitamin’ was coined from the words vital + amine, since the earlier identified compounds had amino group. Vitamins are classified into two groups depending upon their solubility in water or fat namely-fat soluble vitamins and water soluble vitamins.
rows.solution:
XEROPHTHALMIA is caused by a deficiency of VITAMIN A.

Vitamin A is needed to make rhodopsin, the pigment of the retina, and to maintain the epithelial tissues. A mild deficiency shows first as NIGHT BLINDNESS; a prolonged one dries and hardens the cornea — xerophthalmia — and can end in permanent blindness.

TWO SOURCES: FISH LIVER OIL and CARROTS. Milk, butter, eggs and green leafy vegetables serve equally well; the yellow and orange vegetables supply it as carotene, which the body converts.

rows.stem: Why can’t vitamin C be stored in our body ? Name the disease caused by the deficiency of this vitamin.
rows.context: Certain organic compounds are required in small amounts in our diet but their deficiency causes specific disease. These compounds are called vitamins. Most of the vitamins cannot be synthesized in our body but plants can synthesize almost all of them. So they are considered as essential food factors. However, the bacteria of the gut can produce some of the vitamins required by us. All the vitamins are generally available in our diet. The term ‘vitamin’ was coined from the words vital + amine, since the earlier identified compounds had amino group. Vitamins are classified into two groups depending upon their solubility in water or fat namely-fat soluble vitamins and water soluble vitamins.
rows.solution:
Because vitamin C is WATER SOLUBLE, so any excess is READILY EXCRETED IN THE URINE rather than being laid down anywhere.

The body has no fatty tissue in which to hold a water-soluble compound, so no reserve accumulates and a regular dietary supply is required. The FAT-soluble vitamins — A, D, E and K — are the contrast: they are stored in the liver and in adipose tissue and need not be supplied daily.

DISEASE: SCURVY. Vitamin C is needed to make collagen, so without it the gums bleed, wounds fail to heal and the teeth loosen. The deficiency appeared on long sea voyages after only a few weeks without fresh food, and was cured by citrus fruit.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Attempt any five of the following :
(a) Ce(III) is easily oxidised to Ce(IV). Comment.
(b) \(\mathrm{E^{\circ}(Mn^{2+}/Mn)}\) is \(-1.18\) V. Why is this value highly negative in comparison to neighbouring d block elements ?
(c) Which element of 3d series has lowest enthalpy of atomisation and why ?
(d) What happens when sodium chromate is acidified ?
(e) Zn, Cd and Hg are soft metals. Why ?
(f) Why is permanganate titration not carried out in the presence of \(\mathrm{HCl}\) ?
(g) The lower oxides of transition metals are basic whereas the highest are amphoteric/acidic. Give reason.
rows.solution:
(a) Because Ce(IV) has the specially stable \(4f^0\) configuration — the EMPTY f subshell, matching the xenon core.

Cerium(III) is \(4f^1\), and losing that single electron reaches \(4f^0\), so the oxidation is easy. The result is that cerium(IV) is a good oxidising agent in aqueous solution and is used in volumetric analysis, and that cerium is one of the few lanthanoids with a stable state other than \(+3\).

(b) Because \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) has the extra stability of a HALF-FILLED \(3d^5\) subshell.

The potential reflects how readily the metal goes into solution as its \(+2\) ion, and manganese's \(+2\) ion is unusually settled — five parallel electrons, one in each d orbital. That makes the metal give its two electrons up readily, so the reduction potential is highly negative.

(c) ZINC, because its d orbitals are COMPLETELY FILLED.

Enthalpy of atomisation measures the strength of the metallic bonding, and in a transition metal that bonding draws on the \((n-1)d\) electrons as well as the \(ns\). Zinc is \(3d^{10}4s^2\): its d electrons are all paired and contribute nothing, so only the two \(4s\) electrons bond, the interatomic forces are weak, and \(\Delta_a H^{\circ}\) is only about 126 kJ per mole against chromium's 397.

(d) It is converted to SODIUM DICHROMATE, and the colour changes from YELLOW to ORANGE:
\(2\mathrm{Na_2CrO_4} + 2\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na_2Cr_2O_7} + 2\mathrm{Na^+} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The change is a pH-controlled EQUILIBRIUM, not a redox reaction — chromium stays at \(+6\) throughout — and adding alkali reverses it.

(e) Because their d orbitals are COMPLETELY FILLED, so those electrons take no part in the metallic bonding.

Each of zinc, cadmium and mercury is \(d^{10}s^2\), and only the two \(s\) electrons bond. The interatomic forces are correspondingly weak, which shows as softness, as low melting points — mercury is a liquid at room temperature — and as low enthalpies of atomisation.

(f) Because HYDROCHLORIC ACID IS ITSELF OXIDISED by permanganate, to chlorine:
\(2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 16\mathrm{H^+} + 10\mathrm{Cl^-} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 5\mathrm{Cl_2} + 8\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Some of the permanganate is therefore consumed by the medium rather than by the substance being estimated, and the titre comes out too high. Dilute SULPHURIC acid is used instead, since sulphate is already at sulphur's highest oxidation state and cannot be oxidised further.

(g) Because IONIC CHARACTER DECREASES as the oxidation state rises.

In a LOW oxidation state the metal ion is large and weakly polarising, so the metal-oxygen bond is largely IONIC, and an ionic oxide reacts with water to give a base — manganese(II) oxide is basic.

In a HIGH oxidation state the ion is small and highly charged, so it polarises the oxide ion strongly and the bond becomes largely COVALENT. A covalent oxide is acidic — \(\mathrm{Mn_2O_7}\) dissolves to give permanganic acid. The intermediate states, such as \(\mathrm{Mn_3O_4}\) or \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\), are amphoteric.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem:
(i) Ishan’s automobile radiator is filled with 1.0 kg of water. How many grams of ethylene glycol (Molar mass = 62 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)) must Ishan add to get the freezing point of the solution lowered to \(-2.8\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\). \(\mathrm{K_f}\) for water is 1.86 K kg \(\cdot\) \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\).
(ii) What type of deviation from Raoult’s law is shown by ethanol and acetone mixture ? Give reason.
rows.solution:
(i) The freezing point is to be lowered to \(-2{\cdot}8\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), so \(\Delta T_f = 2{\cdot}8\) K. Ethylene glycol is a NON-electrolyte, so \(i = 1\).

Combine the freezing point depression formula with the mass data:
\(\Delta T_f = \dfrac{K_f \times w_B}{M_B \times w_A}\) with \(w_A\) in kilograms
\(2{\cdot}8 = \dfrac{1{\cdot}86 \times w_B}{62 \times 1}\)

\(w_B = \dfrac{2{\cdot}8 \times 62}{1{\cdot}86}\)

\(w_B = 93{\cdot}33\ \mathrm{g}\)

That is the whole point of antifreeze: about 93 g of ethylene glycol in a kilogram of water keeps the radiator liquid nearly three degrees below the freezing point of water, and more would protect it further.

(ii) A mixture of ethanol and acetone shows a POSITIVE DEVIATION from Raoult's law.

REASON. Pure ethanol is extensively hydrogen bonded to itself. Adding acetone puts acetone molecules between the ethanol molecules and breaks some of those hydrogen bonds, and acetone cannot replace them in kind — it has no hydrogen on oxygen to donate, only a lone pair to accept with.

So the ETHANOL-ETHANOL interaction is STRONGER than the ethanol-acetone interaction. Held less tightly, the molecules escape more readily than Raoult's law predicts, and the observed vapour pressure is higher than the ideal value. Mixing is endothermic and the volume expands slightly.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem:
(i) Boiling point of water at 750 mm Hg pressure is \(99.68\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\). How much sucrose (Molar mass = 342 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)) is to be added to 500 g of water such that it boils at \(100\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) ? (\(\mathrm{K_b}\) for water \(= 0.52\) K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)).
(ii) State Henry’s law and write its any one application.
rows.solution:
(i) The water already boils at \(99{\cdot}68\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) at this pressure, so the elevation required is
\(\Delta T_b = 100 - 99{\cdot}68 = 0{\cdot}32\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)

Sucrose is a NON-electrolyte, so \(i = 1\). Combine the boiling point elevation formula with the mass data:
\(\Delta T_b = \dfrac{K_b \times w_B \times 1000}{M_B \times w_A}\)
\(0{\cdot}32 = \dfrac{0{\cdot}52 \times w_B \times 1000}{342 \times 500}\)

\(w_B = \dfrac{0{\cdot}32 \times 342 \times 500}{0{\cdot}52 \times 1000}\)

\(w_B = 105{\cdot}23\ \mathrm{g}\)

Note that the boiling point of pure water is given as \(99{\cdot}68\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), not \(100\) — the pressure is 750 mm Hg rather than 760. Taking \(\Delta T_b\) as zero from a careless reading would leave nothing to calculate.

(ii) HENRY'S LAW. At a constant temperature, the solubility of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of that gas above the surface of the liquid. Equivalently, the partial pressure of the gas in the vapour phase is proportional to its mole fraction in the solution:
\(p = K_{\mathrm{H}}\,x\)

APPLICATION: soft drinks and soda water are SEALED UNDER HIGH PRESSURE of carbon dioxide, which forces more of the gas into solution. Opening the bottle drops the pressure, the solubility falls at once, and the excess gas fizzes out.

Two other applications serve equally well: divers breathe air diluted with helium to reduce the nitrogen dissolved in the blood at depth, and climbers suffer anoxia because the low partial pressure of oxygen at altitude reduces how much dissolves in the blood.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
An organic compound (A) with the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_9H_{10}O}\) forms 2, 4-DNP derivative, reduces Fehling solution and undergoes Cannizzaro reaction. On vigorous oxidation, it gives 1, 2-benzene dicarboxylic acid.
(i) Identify the compound (A) and write its IUPAC name.
(ii) Write the reaction of compound (A) with
(1) 2, 4-Dinitrophenyl hydrazine and
(2) Fehling solution
(iii) Write the equation of compound (A) when it undergoes Cannizzaro reaction.
rows.solution:
(i) Work through the clues. \(\mathrm{C_9H_{10}O}\) with a 2,4-DNP derivative means a CARBONYL compound. Undergoing CANNIZZARO means an ALDEHYDE with NO \(\alpha\)-hydrogen — so the carbon next to the carbonyl bears none, which for an aromatic compound means the \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) is attached directly to the ring.

The decisive clue is the oxidation product: 1,2-BENZENEDICARBOXYLIC ACID. Two carboxyl groups on ADJACENT ring carbons means the molecule had two side chains, ortho to each other, both of which oxidised to \(-\mathrm{COOH}\). One is the \(-\mathrm{CHO}\); the other must account for the remaining two carbons, so it is an ETHYL group.

\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{o}\)-\(\mathrm{C_2H_5{-}C_6H_4{-}CHO}\), and the formula checks: \(\mathrm{C_9H_{10}O}\).
IUPAC name: 2-ETHYLBENZALDEHYDE

(ii)(1) 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine condenses with the carbonyl group, losing water:
\(\mathrm{o\text{-}C_2H_5{-}C_6H_4{-}CHO} + \mathrm{H_2N{-}NH{-}C_6H_3(NO_2)_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{o\text{-}C_2H_5{-}C_6H_4{-}CH{=}N{-}NH{-}C_6H_3(NO_2)_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
The product is the 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone, an orange crystalline solid.

(2) The question states that compound (A) reduces Fehling's solution, but AROMATIC ALDEHYDES DO NOT give the Fehling's test — only aliphatic ones do. The marking scheme records the same point and instructs examiners to award the mark for any attempt at this part [so the clue as printed conflicts with the compound the rest of the question fixes; the identification stands on the Cannizzaro and oxidation clues, which are consistent].

Tollens' reagent, by contrast, DOES work with an aromatic aldehyde, giving a silver mirror.

(iii) 2-Ethylbenzaldehyde has no \(\alpha\)-hydrogen on its carbonyl carbon, so with concentrated alkali it undergoes CANNIZZARO — two molecules react together, one reduced to the alcohol and the other oxidised to the salt of the acid:
\(2\,\mathrm{o\text{-}C_2H_5{-}C_6H_4{-}CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. }\mathrm{NaOH}} \mathrm{o\text{-}C_2H_5{-}C_6H_4{-}CH_2OH} + \mathrm{o\text{-}C_2H_5{-}C_6H_4{-}COO^-Na^+}\)

Note that the ethyl group's hydrogens are NOT \(\alpha\) to the carbonyl — they are on a different ring carbon's substituent — which is why the Cannizzaro route is open.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) Account for the following :
(1) The alpha (\(\alpha\))-hydrogens of aldehydes and ketones are acidic in nature.
(2) Oxidation of aldehydes is easier than ketones.
(ii) Arrange the following in :
(1) Decreasing reactivity towards nucleophilic addition reaction propanal, acetone, benzaldehyde.
(2) Increasing order of boiling point :
Propane, Ethanol, Dimethylether, Propanal
(iii) Give simple chemical test to distinguish between Benzoic acid and Benzaldehyde.
rows.solution:
(i)(1) Because the CARBANION left behind after the \(\alpha\)-hydrogen leaves is stabilised by RESONANCE with the carbonyl group.

The carbonyl group is strongly electron withdrawing, so it pulls density away from the neighbouring carbon and weakens the bond to its hydrogen. More importantly, once that proton has gone the negative charge does not stay on the carbon: it is delocalised onto the carbonyl OXYGEN, an electronegative atom far better able to carry it.

A stabilised conjugate base means a stronger acid — and that acidity is what makes the aldol reaction and the haloform reaction possible.

(2) Because oxidising an ALDEHYDE requires only a \(\mathrm{C-H}\) bond to be broken, while oxidising a KETONE requires a \(\mathrm{C-C}\) bond to be broken.

An aldehyde has a hydrogen ON its carbonyl carbon; removing it and putting an oxygen in its place is easy, which is why even a mild reagent such as Tollens' or Fehling's suffices. A ketone has two carbon substituents there and no hydrogen at all, so oxidising it means CLEAVING the carbon chain — which needs a strong oxidising agent under drastic conditions and gives a mixture of shorter acids.

(ii)(1) Decreasing reactivity towards nucleophilic addition:
PROPANAL > BENZALDEHYDE > ACETONE

Reactivity falls as the carbonyl carbon is made less positive and more crowded. Propanal is an aliphatic ALDEHYDE with just one alkyl group on that carbon. Acetone is a KETONE with TWO, so it is deactivated twice over, both electronically and sterically. Benzaldehyde has only one substituent but it is a phenyl group, which withdraws by resonance — placing it between the two.

(2) Increasing order of boiling point:
PROPANE < DIMETHYL ETHER < PROPANAL < ETHANOL

Propane is non-polar and has only weak dispersion forces. Dimethyl ether is polar, so dipole-dipole attraction adds to those. Propanal is more polar still, its carbonyl group carrying a larger dipole. And only ETHANOL can hydrogen bond to itself, its hydrogen sitting on oxygen — which is by far the strongest of these interactions and puts it top despite its smaller mass.

(iii) Use SODIUM HYDROGENCARBONATE. BENZOIC ACID gives brisk effervescence, releasing carbon dioxide, because it is a stronger acid than carbonic acid; BENZALDEHYDE gives none.

Tollens' reagent serves equally well the other way round — benzaldehyde is oxidised and deposits a silver mirror, while benzoic acid, already at the acid stage, does not react.
